opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that embodied intelligence is fundamentally about interaction. A robot isn't just recognizing an image or answering a question. It's acting in the physical world, and every action changes what it sees next. That closed loop of perception, action, and feedback is exactly what reinforcement learning was designed for.

If you look at how most robot learning works today, a lot of it is imitation learning. You collect teleoperation data, demonstrations from humans, and you train a policy to copy that behavior. That's been very effective at getting things off the ground, and I don't want to dismiss it. But imitation has a ceiling. The robot can only be roughly as good as the demonstrations, and more importantly, it never really learns what happens when it makes a mistake, because the human demonstrator rarely makes those mistakes in the data. Then at deployment, small errors compound, the robot drifts into states it's never seen, and it doesn't know how to recover.

Reinforcement learning addresses that directly. The robot tries things, it fails, it gets a signal about what worked and what didn't, and it improves from its own experience. That's how it can learn robustness and recovery behaviors, and potentially go beyond human performance in speed or precision. We've already seen this pattern in language models. Pretraining on huge amounts of human text gives you a strong prior, but a lot of the recent jumps in reasoning ability came from RL on top of that prior. I think embodied intelligence will follow a similar recipe: large-scale pretraining or imitation to get a good starting policy, then RL to really sharpen it and make it reliable.

The other reason is data. In language, the internet gave us essentially free data. In robotics, there's no internet of robot actions. Human teleoperation is expensive and slow to scale. RL, especially combined with simulation or with robots collecting data autonomously in the real world, is one of the few paths where the system can generate its own learning signal. If we want robots that keep getting better after deployment, rather than being frozen at whatever we taught them, some form of reinforcement learning has to be part of the picture.

Of course, it's hard. Rewards are difficult to define for real tasks, real-world trials are slow and can be unsafe, and the sim-to-real gap is still real. But I see those as engineering and research problems to solve, not reasons to avoid RL. In the long run, I believe the robots that truly work in open environments will be the ones that learn from their own interaction, and that's what reinforcement learning gives us.

r002.rationale: It says imitation has a ceiling and RL lets robots learn from their own failures, recover in unseen states, and potentially exceed human performance.

r003.rationale: It does not identify a shift from local motion control to whole-body control.

r004.rationale: It describes a perception-action-feedback loop in which each action changes what the robot sees next, and says RL improves through the robot’s own interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that embodied intelligence is fundamentally about interacting with the physical world, and the physical world doesn't come with labels. When you're training a language model, you have essentially the entire internet as a corpus of human behavior to imitate. When you're training a robot to manipulate objects or walk over uneven ground, there is no equivalent dataset. You can collect demonstrations, and we do, but demonstrations are expensive, they're limited in coverage, and the moment the robot drifts slightly away from what the demonstrator did, it has no idea how to recover.

Reinforcement learning addresses exactly that gap. Instead of telling the system what to do in every situation, you tell it what outcome you want and let it discover how to get there through trial and error. That matters for two reasons. First, it lets the system find solutions that a human might never have demonstrated, because the robot's body and sensors are different from ours. A quadruped doesn't need to walk like a dog, it needs to walk in whatever way is stable for its own mass distribution and actuators. Second, and I think this is underappreciated, RL produces policies that are robust to perturbation, because the training process itself involves constantly falling off the ideal trajectory and learning to get back on. That closed-loop quality is what you actually need when a real floor is slippery or a real object is heavier than expected.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. RL on real hardware is slow and can break things, so most of the practical progress has come from training in simulation and then transferring to the physical robot. Making that transfer reliable is still one of the hardest problems in the field. But when I look at the breakthroughs in legged locomotion over the past several years, nearly all of them came from RL in simulation. That tells me the approach is not a research curiosity anymore, it's becoming the default way you get an agent to acquire physical skills.

So to me, RL is important because it's the learning paradigm that most closely matches what embodied intelligence actually is: an agent acting in the world, observing consequences, and improving. Imitation gets you started, but RL is what gets you competence.

r002.rationale: It says RL can find solutions not demonstrated by humans and handle situations beyond demonstrations, while imitation only gets the system started.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify a shift from local motion control to whole-body control.

r004.rationale: It mentions sensors and observing consequences, but does not state that the robot’s visual observations must be part of the RL interaction loop.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is important because embodied intelligence is fundamentally about acting and learning from the consequences. A robot doesn’t just need to recognize what’s in front of it. It needs to decide what to do, observe how the world responds, and adjust its behavior over time.

Take picking up a cup. Recognizing the cup is only part of the problem. How firmly should you grip it? What happens if it slips? How should you change your movement if it’s heavier than expected? Reinforcement learning gives us a framework for learning those decisions through interaction, with success measured over a sequence of actions.

But I wouldn’t say reinforcement learning alone is enough. Exploration on physical hardware can be slow, expensive, and risky. So the practical question is how to combine it with demonstrations, simulation, and useful prior knowledge. To me, its key role is helping an embodied system improve beyond what it was explicitly shown—to adapt its behavior based on what actually works.

r004.rationale: It describes observing the world during interaction, but does not state that training uses the robot’s visual observations in the interaction loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is important because embodied intelligence is fundamentally about acting and learning from the consequences. An agent needs to understand not only what is in front of it, but what will happen if it moves, touches something, or applies a certain amount of force.

You can learn a lot from demonstrations, but demonstrations cannot cover every situation. When a robot encounters an unfamiliar object or makes a small mistake, it needs a way to adjust its behavior. Reinforcement learning provides a framework for that: try an action, receive feedback, and improve toward a goal over time.

The challenge is making this process efficient and safe in the physical world. So I see reinforcement learning working together with perception, imitation learning, and models of the environment. Those give the robot a useful starting point; interaction helps it turn that knowledge into reliable behavior.
